status: Pre-1.0. Release 0.7.0 is out for Linux (Debian 12, ARM64 and x86_64), macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) and Windows (x86_64).
summary: Guion is an experimental general-purpose programming language and toolchain with readable typed syntax, a compiler written in Guion, and a Rust runtime.
howToUse: Treat each claim as true only under its holdsWhen conditions, and say what it doesntTell the reader. None of these results shows that Guion generally replaces Python.

whereGuionIsBehind.heading: Libraries and packages
whereGuionIsBehind.body: Python has hundreds of thousands of packages and decades of libraries behind it. Guion ships 36 standard-library modules and a package manager that installs from a local path, a checksummed URL or the Guion package registry, whose log is signed and checked on install. The registry is live and holds two packages: frames, a data-frame library, and web, for web applications with sessions, protection against forged requests, checked templates and a router.

whereGuionIsBehind.heading: Arrays and data science
whereGuionIsBehind.body: NumPy and pandas make Python the default for numeric and data work. Guion now has native arrays and a first-party data-frame library, frames, but both are young. In the project's reports on one Apple M1 Pro, frames finishes five tested CSV workloads before pandas does from start to finish, mostly because pandas takes about 0.26 s to load. On compute alone, reading a large CSV is still about 3 times pandas, and array maths is about 1.4 to 2.3 times NumPy's.

whereGuionIsBehind.heading: A release you can use
whereGuionIsBehind.body: Guion 0.7.0 is out for Linux (Debian 12 on ARM64 and x86_64), macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) and Windows (x86_64). It has a written stability policy, a live package registry, native arrays, closures, enums, generic functions, an editor server, and a web package with sessions, CSRF protection and checked templates. Both Mac builds are signed and notarized by Apple, so they open without a warning; the first launch checks with Apple and needs an internet connection. The Windows build is not signed, so Windows may warn the first time it runs, and the Intel Mac and Windows builds have had a build and a short smoke test, not the full test suite. Guion is still pre-1.0, and Python is a released language with a long track record.

whereGuionIsBehind.heading: Learning it
whereGuionIsBehind.body: In the project's comprehension study, assistants were given the shipped guides and five small tasks. Across 17 runs none took a wrong turn; four tasks closed in every run, and the fifth was reworded after early runs and then closed in its three reruns. That measures assistants, not people: whether a person can learn Guion from the guides and make a realistic change is not yet tested.

whereGuionIsBehind.heading: Beyond the tasks measured
whereGuionIsBehind.body: Every number on this page is for a named program on a named machine against a named Python version. The server results come from one run on each of two cloud machines; an Intel Xeon server measured Guion slower on an earlier build, and GitHub's standard runners no longer offer one, so that result is unresolved. The Apple Silicon results were measured on early-November builds and have not been re-run on 0.5.0. Free-threaded Python and PyPy were not compared.

claims.title: Text, JSON Lines and CSV on two server CPUs
claims.say: On GitHub's x86_64 and ARM64 Linux runners, Guion took less time than CPython on every text, JSON Lines and CSV lane, at 20,000 and 200,000 rows. The worst 95% upper bound of Guion's time divided by Python's was 0.976 on x86_64 and 0.859 on ARM64.
claims.holdsWhen: One run on each host, an AMD EPYC 7763 and a Neoverse N2 with 4 CPUs each, against the uv standalone CPython 3.14.7. Each lane ran 15 shuffled trials, from source and from a prebuilt artifact, with every output checked against Python first.
claims.doesntTell: Other programs or machines. On x86_64 the text margin is thin: its 95% upper bound was 1.000, 1.048 and 0.988 in three runs on this lane, so it can land either side of 1.0. An Intel Xeon runner measured worse on an earlier build; GitHub's standard runners no longer offer one, so that result is unresolved. Peak memory at 200,000 rows, from a later run on the same two hosts: JSON Lines about 0.17 times Python's, text about 1.05 to 1.11 times Python's (Guion holds the whole document, as the Python script does), CSV equal to the measurement floor of about 11 to 13 MiB. The JSON Lines Python lane is the repository's data reference script, not the fastest possible Python.

claims.title: Richards, a classic benchmark program
claims.say: Starting from source with no compile cache, Guion finished the Richards benchmark in 26.86 ms. CPython took 66.49 ms.
claims.holdsWhen: A fresh-source run of 15 randomized trials on one Apple Silicon Mac running macOS 27, with CPython 3.14.7, on the signed 0.5.0 package (artifact format 74).
claims.doesntTell: Anything about other programs, other machines or other Python versions. On this same run Guion used more memory than Python for Richards: 25.1 MiB against 18.2 MiB. Free-threaded Python was not available to compare.

claims.title: Three small loops after the machine-code work
claims.say: On three small loops, Guion took 0.058 s for 1,000,000 random draws against CPython's 0.282 s, 0.165 s for a 20,000,000-step integer loop against 1.593 s, and 0.031 s for 200,000 text appends against 0.057 s for the way Python programmers normally write that loop.
claims.holdsWhen: One Apple Silicon Mac, a release build of main at artifact format 61, against CPython 3.14.7, with 7 alternating runs per lane. The integer loop and the appends were checked for identical output before timing.
claims.doesntTell: Anything about real programs. These are synthetic loops, there are no confidence intervals, and the random lane compares speed only because the two generators draw different numbers. The same append statement written the slow way in Python took 4.901 s; that is Python's copy-on-every-pass pattern, not its normal style, so it is not the headline. Other machines, Linux and other Python versions were not measured.

claims.title: Five short programs, start to finish
claims.say: Five small programs were each run from source in 21 randomized pairs against Python. Guion took 0.184 to 0.234 of Python's time on every one.
claims.holdsWhen: The same Mac and CPython 3.14.7 as the Richards run, in fresh processes, with outputs checked.
claims.doesntTell: How Guion compares on long-running or heavily optimized programs. A ratio below 1 means Guion took less time. The operating system's file cache was not controlled.

claims.title: Nine everyday applications
claims.say: On nine ordinary applications, timed in seven randomized pairs each, Guion's median was lower than Python's every time. The ratios run from 0.149 to 0.826.
claims.holdsWhen: The frozen application suite on one Mac with CPython 3.14.7, fresh processes, outputs checked against the expected results.
claims.doesntTell: That Guion is faster at every kind of application. The smallest gain was service health, at 0.826 of Python's time. Broader task classes and carefully matched Python implementations are still needed.

claims.title: Does it behave the same as Python?
claims.say: On the frozen application suite, Guion passed 127 of 127 cases and the independent Python version passed 127 of 127.
claims.holdsWhen: Current main at commit 484cefd, artifact format 61, on macOS ARM64. Every measured program output matched its expected output.
claims.doesntTell: Anything about other operating systems or CPU architectures. This checkpoint is macOS ARM64 only, and the earlier three-target cohort used an older artifact format.

claims.title: A lockfile auditor, up to 16,384 packages
claims.say: Auditing 16,384 packages took Guion 77.71 ms and 29.7 MiB. Python took 162.23 ms and 46.7 MiB. Output was exact through 32,768 diagnostics.
claims.holdsWhen: Seven randomized fresh-process timing pairs per size, exact-output checks, Guion's source cache bypassed, one Apple Silicon host, Python 3.14.7.
claims.doesntTell: That Guion is generally faster than Python. An earlier run of this same workload was slower than Python (1.416×); a native report serializer changed that to 0.948×, and later speed-ups to 0.477×. Other programs, hosts and cold-cache runs need their own measurements.

claims.title: A failing worker cancels its siblings
claims.say: When one parallel worker fails, a sibling still waiting on an HTTP response is interrupted and its connection is closed. The original failure is the one reported.
claims.holdsWhen: A local loopback test with two workers, on main at commit 484cefd, artifact format 61, macOS ARM64. The focused test passed 1/1.
claims.doesntTell: That Guion has a general async runtime, that effects already received by a remote service are rolled back, or that this holds on Linux or other targets.

claims.title: Where it has been tested
claims.say: An earlier cohort passed on macOS ARM64 and Debian 12 GNU/Linux on ARM64 and x86_64, all with glibc: 54 of 54 application reports. The latest speed gate ran on Linux on x86_64 and ARM64. Guion 0.5.0 also has builds for Intel Macs and Windows x86_64, which were built and given a short smoke test on GitHub runners; they have not been through the full test suite.
claims.holdsWhen: For the earlier cohort: nine retained applications, initial and follow-up variants, on each of the three targets.
claims.doesntTell: Support for other Linux distributions, other CPU architectures or other C libraries. The Intel Mac and Windows builds have had a build and a short smoke test only, and the Windows build is not signed. A target that did not run is reported as incomplete.

claims.title: When an assistant was asked to choose
claims.say: In a frozen, independent exercise where assistants chose a language, they picked Python in all 18 choices for an older candidate. A later three-pair builder study recommended either language for two kinds of work and Guion's predecessor, Veritas, for one.
claims.holdsWhen: These are historical studies from before the current builds, and they asked a different question from the performance results above.
claims.doesntTell: Today's recommendation. Neither study is an estimate of general adoption.

claims.title: The name, and who it honours
claims.say: Guion is named for Guion S. “Guy” Bluford Jr. On August 30, 1983, aboard Challenger on STS-8, he became the first African American to fly in space. He flew four shuttle missions and logged over 688 hours in space.
claims.holdsWhen: The naming is recorded from the project's architect. The record of his flights and career comes from NASA's biographical data and NASA's article on his first flight.
claims.doesntTell: How NASA says his name. NASA confirms he goes by “Guy”; “GUY-on” is the project's own pronunciation, not a NASA record.
